description: We are a group of amateur students who try to make use of complex NASA scientific data to make simpler user, friendly interactive tools.
summary:
ARES (Advanced Reconnaissance and Exploration System) is an interactive Mars exploration dashboard developed to support the planning and analysis of potential rover and astronaut exploration routes on Mars, specifically in the area around gale crater. It integrates real NASA MOLA elevation data and THEMIS thermal observations to provide coordinate-based terrain elevation and surface temperature information. The website of this dashboard can only be properly viewed in pc devices like computers or laptop and not mobile devices.

Users can place waypoints, examine environmental conditions, analyse routes and monitor simulated EVA suit telemetry, including oxygen and battery levels. By combining topographic and thermal information in one interface, ARES demonstrates how scientific datasets can contribute to more informed exploration planning.

The project aims to make Mars exploration data more accessible, understandable and useful for mission-planning concepts. It also highlights the importance of terrain awareness and environmental analysis when considering future human and robotic exploration of Mars.
details:
Project Details: ARES (Advanced Reconnaissance and Exploration System)

ARES is an interactive Mars exploration and mission-planning dashboard designed to help users examine Martian surface conditions and analyze potential exploration routes. It combines topographical and thermal information with route-planning tools in a single interface.

How It Works

ARES integrates real elevation measurements from NASA's Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) dataset and thermal observations from the Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS) aboard NASA's Mars Odyssey spacecraft.

Users can interact with the Martian map and place multiple waypoints to examine important environmental and geographical parameters, including:

  • Elevation: Retrieves coordinate-based surface elevation measurements using MOLA data.
  • Temperature: Displays THEMIS surface brightness-temperature observations within the available data coverage.
  • Distance: Calculates the distance along a selected exploration route.
  • Estimated Travel Time: Estimates the time required to complete a route using the system's movement model.
  • Slope: Analyses terrain gradients along the selected route using elevation information, helping users understand changes in surface steepness.

ARES also displays simulated Extravehicular Activity (EVA) suit telemetry, including oxygen and battery levels, to demonstrate how mission resources could be monitored during exploration planning.

Benefits and Intended Impact

ARES brings different types of Martian scientific information into one accessible interface. By combining elevation, temperature, distance, travel-time estimates and slope analysis, it helps users understand the geographical and environmental factors involved in selecting potential exploration routes.

Its intended impact is to demonstrate how planetary datasets and computational tools can contribute to the conceptual planning of future robotic and human exploration missions.

Technology and Development

The project was developed using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Leaflet.js provides interactive mapping, while IndexedDB supports local storage of scientific datasets. NASA planetary datasets were processed and integrated into the application. The project is publicly hosted through GitHub Pages.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of ARES is its integration of scientific data retrieval, interactive mapping, waypoint selection, route calculations and simulated mission telemetry within one dashboard. Rather than presenting planetary information as separate scientific records, ARES transforms it into an interactive mission-planning experience.

Scientific Data Coverage and Limitations

ARES integrates two planetary science datasets: the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) elevation dataset and the Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS) thermal observation dataset.

1. MOLA Elevation Data

ARES uses the MOLA 128 pixels-per-degree topography dataset, specifically the file megt00n090hb.img, obtained from the NASA Planetary Data System.

The integrated dataset covers:

  • Latitude: 0° to 44° South
  • Longitude: 90°E to 180°E

ARES retrieves actual MOLA elevation measurements for supported coordinates within this geographical region. Coordinates outside this coverage are distinguished from actual scientific measurements using demonstration values.

2. THEMIS Thermal Data

ARES uses a THEMIS thermal observation from NASA's Mars Odyssey spacecraft, specifically observation I01443004PBT.

The integrated observation uses a sinusoidal map projection centered at approximately 139.516°E longitude. Its valid geographical footprint is approximately:

  • Latitude: 12.909° South to 5.240° North
  • Longitude: 137.983°E to 140.990°E

ARES retrieves thermal brightness-temperature values from valid pixels within this observation's coverage. These values represent surface brightness temperature, not atmospheric or astronaut air temperature.

3. Data Coverage and Reliability

MOLA and THEMIS have different geographical coverage areas. Consequently, a coordinate may have valid MOLA elevation data but no corresponding THEMIS thermal observation, or vice versa.

ARES distinguishes actual scientific measurements from demonstration values outside supported data coverage. This approach helps maintain transparency about data availability and avoids presenting unsupported estimates as verified planetary observations.

The application is a conceptual exploration and mission-planning tool, not a certified navigation or astronaut-safety system. It can only be operated and properly viewed in pc devices like computer and laptop and not mobile devices.

Factors Considered

Our team considered scientific data reliability, coordinate accuracy, usability, performance and the geographical limitations of available observations. MOLA and THEMIS have different coverage areas, so ARES distinguishes actual scientific readings from demonstration values outside supported data coverage.

We also considered terrain variation, surface temperature, route distance, estimated travel time and slope when designing the exploration-analysis system.

ARES is a conceptual exploration-planning tool, not a certified mission-navigation or astronaut-safety system.
